title: Meta introduces Spaces: custom app views built by your Muse agent
content:
Today, we’re introducing spaces, an interactive way to build a more personalized Muse. A space is a custom experience you create inside Muse by describing your idea, like a holiday gift tracker, a daily word game, or a planning board for your next DIY project. It’s shaped around your routines, goals, and interests, and can be as practical or entertaining as you want. Every space you create becomes part of Muse, so you can keep it where you want and come back to it any time.
From An Idea to Something Real
Have an idea you’ve been meaning to try? Tell Muse about it, and it builds it for you. Your initial idea is just the starting point. As you use your space, you can keep adjusting it with Muse, whether that’s adding what’s missing, trying a new look, or changing how it works.
You can also choose where your spaces live in Muse. Add them to your sidebar, move them into your main tabs, hide the ones you don’t need right now, and schedule when they appear. For example, keep your weekly planner up front during the workweek, then swap it for your weekend plans on Saturday.
What You Can Build
Spaces can help you get things done, have a little fun, or give your creative projects a home. Here are a few ideas:
- A shopping hub that brings holiday and birthday gift ideas, wishlists from Instagram saves, and your Marketplace listings and buyer messages into one view
- A school dashboard that finds the events relevant to your kids in school emails and adds them to your calendar
- A music tracker for the artists you love, with new releases and upcoming shows
- A wedding planner with your RSVP list, vendor invoices, and to-dos
- A trivia game that quizzes you on your favorite movies, music, or sports team
- A podcast studio to keep your episode ideas, research, and scripts together
- An order tracker for your small business, with new orders, customer messages and what needs to ship today
- A client hub for your freelance work, with projects, deadlines, and invoices
- A trip planner with your flights, hotel, reservations and a day-by-day itinerary.
Got a half-finished idea sitting in your notes app, a spreadsheet you keep meaning to clean up, or a hobby you want to dive into? Chances are you can turn it into a space.
A Space That Keeps Up With You
Your spaces are personal from the start. Connect the apps you use, and your spaces keep themselves up to date in the background, so new concert dates, price changes, or savings progress show up without you having to ask. You can check things off, add notes, and make edits right in your space, and everything will be there when you return.
Looking Ahead
Starting today, spaces are available everywhere Muse is available. We’re also exploring ways for you to share your spaces with others to build a more collaborative experience in Muse.
We’re also rolling out specialized versions of our models to Muse, trained with learnings from Muse Wonder, to make your overall experience even better.

report.summary: Meta’s Muse agent now lets users describe custom app-like Spaces—trackers, planners, games—that it builds and keeps updated inside Muse.
report.background: Meta’s Spaces launch is part of a broader shift in AI assistants from simple chat interfaces toward agentic, personalized software. Instead of asking users to assemble spreadsheets, calendars, and note apps, Muse uses natural-language instructions to generate lightweight interactive views inside the assistant. The move follows growing competition among AI platforms to turn chatbots into hubs for tasks, content, and commerce. Meta’s ecosystem—Instagram saves, Marketplace listings, messaging, and calendar data—gives Spaces a potential advantage in personalization. At the same time, the product raises questions about data access, reliability, and lock-in. Meta says it is also bringing specialized models trained with learnings from Muse Wonder, suggesting Spaces is both a consumer feature and a testbed for agent-generated interfaces.
key_points: Users create a Space by describing an idea—such as a gift tracker, trivia game, or wedding planner—and Muse builds an interactive experience. They can then refine it conversationally by adding features, changing its look, or adjusting how it works. This turns the assistant from a Q&A tool into a lightweight no-code app builder for personal use.

Spaces can be placed in the sidebar, moved into main tabs, hidden, or scheduled to appear at certain times. A weekly planner can surface during the workweek and give way to weekend plans on Saturday. This makes Spaces feel less like separate apps and more like adaptable modules inside the Muse interface.

Connected apps keep Spaces updated in the background, so concert dates, price changes, savings progress, or Instagram wishlists can refresh without manual checks. Users can also check off items, add notes, and edit content directly. The value depends on which connectors Meta supports and how reliably those background updates work.

Meta lists uses ranging from a school dashboard that extracts events from emails to a small-business order tracker, freelance client hub, podcast studio, and trip planner. The common thread is consolidating scattered information and tasks into one view, rather than replacing full-featured professional software.

Spaces are available everywhere Muse is available, and Meta is exploring sharing and collaborative experiences. It is also rolling out specialized Muse models trained with learnings from Muse Wonder. That signals faster iteration on personalized interfaces and a possible social layer for agent-built mini-apps.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Spaces pushes assistants toward generative UI and agent-built micro-apps, intensifying competition with OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and others experimenting with artifacts, apps, and connectors. Developers may see new demand for APIs, connectors, and agent orchestration, while simple standalone utilities face pressure to become integrations. Regular users get a lower barrier to personalized tools, but must weigh convenience against data permissions, reliability, and lock-in to Meta’s ecosystem. The biggest test is whether Muse can build trustworthy Spaces that update correctly without exposing sensitive email, shopping, or business data. If it works, the assistant becomes a personal software platform.
report.tools: To follow the trend, watch Meta Muse and Spaces as the proprietary reference. For hands-on experimentation, try Vercel AI SDK’s generative UI, LangGraph/LangChain for agent workflows, CopilotKit for in-app agents, and OpenUI for natural-language interface generation. Compare with Anthropic’s Artifacts and OpenAI’s app/connector efforts. Developers should study Muse’s connector model and privacy controls.
